Both are pupil abnormalities without ptosis.
Both cause diplopia without affecting the lid.
A pupil finding with no lid component.
Horner syndrome and third nerve palsy

Reassure and review in six months
Delay costs central vision that treatment could save.
Supplements slow progression in dry disease; they do not treat active wet disease.
Urgent referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy
Correct. The wet form is treatable and the window matters.

A cause of Horner syndrome, but not the one signalled by acute neck pain after trauma.
Affects the third nerve and spares the pupil.
Correct. Painful Horner syndrome of sudden onset is a dissection until proven otherwise.

An absent reflex is never a normal variant.
Delay risks irreversible amblyopia and, if it is a tumour, far worse.
Does not address the ocular finding.
Correct. An absent red reflex demands urgent assessment — cataract and retinoblastoma both present this way.

Photophobia and cells, without the autonomic disturbance.
Inferior rectus entrapment in a floor fracture
Correct. Restricted upgaze with severe pain and AUTONOMIC DISTURBANCE — bradycardia and vomiting on attempted movement — is the entrapment picture.
Bruising and swelling, without restricted upgaze or bradycardia.

Continue lid hygiene alone for three months
Two weeks without improvement is the stated point to escalate.

Immediately, and it requires general anaesthesia
It is an outpatient procedure without anaesthesia.
One hour, and renal function must be checked
Transit is seconds, not an hour.
Ten to fifteen seconds, and it contains no iodine
Correct — the absence of iodine matters for patients who report contrast allergy.

Routine, and it settles in two to four weeks.

opts: Correct — the longer eye has a thinner, more vulnerable peripheral retina.
A childhood malignancy unrelated to refractive error.
An infectious cicatricial disease unrelated to refraction.
Angle closure is associated with the SHORT, hyperopic eye.

Depresses the eye and is supplied by the third nerve.

Depresses the adducted eye and is supplied by the fourth nerve.

Correct. Measuring the intraocular pressure confirms the diagnosis and is the immediate step.
Discharge with topical antibiotic eye drops
There is no infection, and discharge would be sight-threatening.

Blunt force from a fist or ball

A small pupil with ptosis and anhidrosis.

opts: Correct. Watery discharge, follicles, a tender preauricular node, and one eye then the other after a cold.

When it is acquired in adulthood

That belongs to the amaurosis fugax pathway.
Thyroid disease causes proptosis rather than scleritis.

Glasses cannot be prescribed at this age
Refractive correction is available at any age.
Treatment works less well as maturity approaches

Misdirected lashes can occur without the lid itself rotating; here the lid margin is turned in.
The lid margin turns OUT, exposing the inner surface and producing TEARING rather than a foreign body sensation.
Excess folds of lid skin, which produces heaviness rather than lashes against the cornea.

A.q: A 31-year-old woman has had a painless, firm nodule in her upper lid for six weeks. Warm compresses and lid massage for a month have not reduced it. Vision is unaffected. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Refer to ophthalmology for steroid injection or curettage
Correct. Conservative measures come first; a lesion that has not resolved goes on for intralesional steroid or curettage.
Incise and drain it in clinic
Incision and drainage is the hordeolum pathway; a chalazion is curetted or injected by ophthalmology.
Continue warm compresses for a further six months
Improvement can take months, but a lesion persisting beyond two to three months warrants referral rather than more of the same.
A chalazion is a STERILE gland obstruction, so antibiotics do not address it.

Associated with cataract and raised pressure.

opts: Refer for immediate surgical exploration of the globe
Not required for a superficial corneal foreign body.
Leave it and review in a week
Retained metal and rust cause ongoing inflammation.
Remove it and the rust ring, then antibiotics
Correct — the rust ring is removed too, as it perpetuates inflammation.
Irrigation does not dislodge an embedded fragment.

A.q: An 18-year-old woman has had a swelling of her left upper eyelid for 10 days. For the first day or two it was red and mildly painful; it is now painless but has grown. There has been no drainage, no change in vision and no itching. She has been well otherwise. Vital signs are normal, extraocular movements are intact and the pupils are equal and reactive. The left upper lid carries a 1.5 cm round, non-tender, mildly erythematous mass with no drainage. The underside of the lid is greyish-red. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Inflammation of the lid MARGIN with crusting at the lash bases and a frothy tear film, not a discrete 1.5 cm nodule.
Correct. A sterile obstruction of a meibomian gland: it builds over days to weeks and the mature lesion is NON-tender, which is what the painless second week tells you.
Infection of the lacrimal sac, which swells the NASAL aspect of the LOWER lid below the medial canthal tendon and expresses pus from the punctum.
An acute staphylococcal infection of a lid gland. It appears within about 24 hours and stays TENDER, where this became painless as it grew.

opts: Correct — it distinguishes a dendrite from an ulcer from punctate disease, and each is treated differently.

The pathology here is corneal, not retinal.

Painful on movement with an afferent pupillary defect.

Causes viral conjunctivitis rather than a suppurative ulcer.

Not implied by a lid laceration.

Correct — the rebleed risk peaks in the first three to five days.
Development of a cataract within 48 hours

A later concern rather than the reason for close monitoring.
An inflammatory demyelinating condition, unrelated to trauma.

Magnetic resonance imaging of brain and orbits

Rigid shield, nil by mouth, urgent referral

Comfort is not the stated purpose.
So the patient does not strain
Correct — straining raises pressure on an open eye.

Correct — it rests the ciliary body and keeps the iris from adhering to the lens.

That there is no deeper injury

The melanoma is raised; the nevus flat with cysts

Two weeks without improvement is the trigger to escalate.
Refer to ophthalmology for incision and drainage
Correct — persistence beyond two weeks is the stated threshold.
Curettage is the chalazion pathway, and by a specialist.

Correct. Refer to ophthalmology if several weeks of treatment fail.
It resolves spontaneously within a month
Blepharitis is not a surgical condition.
It resolves once the associated rosacea is treated
Treating rosacea helps, but the lid disease remains chronic.

opts: Correct. Drusen and pigment change with gradual central loss over years.
Causes generalised blur and glare rather than distortion of straight lines.
Takes the peripheral field first and spares central acuity until late.
Presents with RAPID distortion and subretinal haemorrhage or fluid.

C.q: A 23-year-old man has severe purulent conjunctivitis with a palpable preauricular node. Why is the node significant here?
opts: It is an incidental finding of no significance
It is the finding that changes the diagnosis.
Bacterial conjunctivitis otherwise lacks a node
Correct. Severe purulent discharge WITH a node points to gonococcal disease.
A node is typical of viral disease, but the discharge here is severely purulent.
That presents with proptosis and painful restricted movement.

Topical anaesthetic drops to take home
Repeated topical anaesthetic is toxic to the epithelium and delays healing.

A tight pressure patch for a week
Patching is no longer routine and is avoided in contact lens wearers.

Correct — delay risks metastatic spread. Not only a threat to sight.
The other eye will be affected within a week
Bilaterality reflects germline status rather than rapid spread.
The squint is a sign, not the reason for urgency.

C.q: A 72-year-old woman with dry macular degeneration is given a grid of straight lines to check at home. What is she being asked to detect?
opts: Correct — the Amsler grid is a self-monitoring tool for exactly that change. That suggests conversion to the wet form.
That is assessed by examination, not by a grid.
The grid tests central vision only.

C.q: A 36-year-old man with inflammatory dacryoadenitis is started on corticosteroids. Within what period should inflammatory disease respond?

Inflammatory disease is precisely what steroids treat here.
Longer than the expected response window.
Correct — failure to respond in that window prompts reconsideration.

C.q: Which infection is classically associated with light-near dissociation and small irregular pupils?
opts: Causes facial palsy among other neurological features, not this pupil.
Causes chorioretinitis rather than a pupil abnormality.
Correct — neurosyphilis is the classic association.

C.q: A 46-year-old man has a flat, pigmented iris lesion that has been unchanged on photographs over five years, with no distortion of the pupil. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Not a treatment for a benign iris nevus.
Correct. Documented stability over years supports a benign nevus.
Grossly disproportionate to a stable, flat lesion.
Reserved for lesions with malignant features.

C.q: A 76-year-old man with entropion has developed a corneal epithelial defect from lash contact. What does this change?
opts: Correct — the slit lamp question in these lid malpositions is always whether the cornea has been affected. Which is what the examination looks for.
Corneal involvement makes surgery more pressing, not less.
Lubrication remains part of protecting the surface.
It confirms the diagnosis is ectropion
Ectropion turns the lid outward and does not bring lashes onto the cornea.

C.q: A 54-year-old man has sudden vision loss that is PAINFUL. Which two diagnoses in this block should come to mind first?
opts: Amaurosis is transient and painless; papilledema causes headache rather than eye pain.
Non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy and branch artery occlusion
Both painless, and both produce a field defect rather than pain.
Central retinal artery occlusion and retinal detachment
Both are painless; the artery occlusion is instant and the detachment is preceded by flashes.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma and optic neuritis
Correct — those are the two painful causes; the rest are painless.

C.q: A 56-year-old woman has confirmed acute angle-closure glaucoma. Which anatomical feature predisposed her to it?
opts: Correct — a crowded angle is what allows closure when the pupil dilates.
A deep chamber protects against angle closure.
Long eyes are myopic and are at LOWER risk of angle closure.
Relevant to pressure measurement rather than to angle closure.

C.q: A 29-year-old patient has two days of painful red eyes and blurred vision. The pain is a deep ache with sensitivity to light (photophobia). There is no discharge and no recent trauma. The medical history includes ankylosing spondylitis. Examination shows conjunctival injection primarily around the limbus, a sluggish pupillary response, and cells in the anterior chamber on slit-lamp examination. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Allergic disease itches and does not produce anterior chamber cells.
There is no bacterial infection; the discharge is absent.
Correct, with a cycloplegic for comfort and to prevent synechiae.
Supportive only, and they do nothing for intraocular inflammation.
C.cite: CMS I Common Ophthalmological Disorders, Slide 63

C.q: A 63-year-old man is found on routine examination to have a raised pigmented choroidal lesion with orange pigment and associated subretinal fluid. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Photograph and review in two years
Those risk features warrant urgent assessment.
Reassure, as choroidal pigmentation is common
Common, but not with orange pigment and subretinal fluid.
Correct. Orange pigment, thickness and subretinal fluid are the features that separate melanoma from a benign nevus.

D.q: A 62-year-old man is found on screening to have an intraocular pressure of 26 mm Hg in both eyes with an enlarged optic cup. He has no symptoms. Which visual field is lost first?

Central loss occurs late in the disease.
Correct. Central acuity is preserved until late, which is why it is found on screening rather than by the patient.
The temporal field of one eye only
That pattern suggests a chiasmal lesion.

opts: The optic nerve or extensive retina
Correct — it separates neural causes from media opacities.
A media opacity rather than a neural lesion.
A cataract reduces light but does not usually produce a true afferent defect.
Blur does not alter afferent conduction.

opts: Correct. A white eye with full painless movements and normal vision is the single most useful discrimination in this block.
The globe would be red with proptosis, painful restricted movement, and possibly an afferent pupillary defect.
Localises to the lacrimal sac below the medial canthal tendon.
A discrete tender nodule at the lid margin rather than diffuse lid swelling.

Assessed by field testing and imaging.
The lids, cornea, conjunctiva, sclera and iris

D.q: A 47-year-old man develops floaters, flashes and a curtain over his vision two weeks after blunt ocular trauma. Which type of detachment is most likely?
opts: Fluid accumulates without a break, usually from inflammation or tumour.
Fibrovascular membranes pull the retina off, classically in diabetes.
Correct — a retinal break allows fluid beneath the retina, and trauma is a common cause.
Not the mechanism following a discrete injury.

A raised opening pressure with normal constituents

The pressure is raised, which is the point.

D.q: A 34-year-old woman has reduced vision in the left eye. On the swinging flashlight test, both pupils constrict when the light is shone in the right eye, but both DILATE when the light is swung to the left eye. What does this indicate?
opts: A left relative afferent pupillary defect
Correct. The left optic nerve conducts less well, so swinging to it is a net reduction in light input.
That gives a small pupil with ptosis, and the light reaction is preserved.
An efferent defect on the left
An efferent lesion affects only the pupil on the damaged side; here both pupils behave symmetrically.
An Adie tonic pupil on the left
That is a large pupil with a slow, tonic near response.

A better prognosis than unilateral disease
Bilateral disease is germline and carries added risk, not a better outlook.
Correct — bilateral disease is germline, with implications for siblings and for second malignancies.

Surgery is one risk among several.

D.q: A 41-year-old man is found to have a relative afferent pupillary defect. Which of the following would explain it?

Blurred focus does not alter afferent conduction.
Correct — a defect of the afferent pathway, which is the optic nerve.
An efferent problem; the pupil on that side may be fixed but the swinging test is not affected this way.

D.q: A 3-year-old boy has an eye that turns inward. The cover test shows the left eye moving out to take up fixation when the right is covered. What is the most appropriate next step?

A constant manifest deviation does not resolve on its own.
Prescribe reading glasses and review in a year
Refraction may be part of treatment, but the referral comes first.
Correct. Manifest misalignment in a child needs assessment to prevent amblyopia.

D.q: In roughly what fraction of FULL-THICKNESS lid lacerations is there an accompanying corneal laceration or globe rupture?
opts: An order of magnitude below the stated fraction.
Correct — which is why the globe is examined in every case.

D.q: Which muscle does the fourth cranial nerve supply, and what is its action?

That is supplied by the third nerve.
Lateral rectus, which abducts the eye
Superior oblique, which depresses the adducted eye
Correct — hence vertical diplopia worse on downgaze.
Medial rectus, which adducts the eye
Third nerve, and it moves the globe horizontally rather than vertically.

D.q: A 26-year-old woman is diagnosed with adult inclusion conjunctivitis. Besides treating her eye, what else must be addressed?

Topical treatment alone leaves the genital infection untreated.

D.q: A 60-year-old man has a small, flat, uniformly pigmented choroidal lesion with drusen on its surface and no subretinal fluid. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reserved for lesions with malignant features.
Grossly disproportionate for a lesion with benign features.
Correct. Flatness, drusen and absent fluid all favour a benign nevus.

opts: Correct — uveal melanoma spreads haematogenously, and the liver is the classic site.
A site for cutaneous melanoma spread, but not the classic one here.
The uvea has no lymphatic drainage, which is why spread is haematogenous.
Involved in many malignancies but not the classic site for this one.

D.q: A 52-year-old patient has a burning sensation in both eyes. There has been no trauma and no contact with anyone with similar symptoms. Examination shows red, inflamed lid margins with greasy, matted lashes and dandruff-like debris at their bases. The conjunctivae are clear and there is no corneal involvement. Colonisation with which organism is found in a significant fraction of patients with this condition?
opts: Correct. Blepharitis is associated with S. aureus, and with rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis.
The organism of contact-lens-related corneal ulcer, not blepharitis.
A cause of bacterial conjunctivitis rather than chronic lid margin disease.
Causes adult inclusion conjunctivitis and trachoma, with follicles and a preauricular node rather than lid-margin scurf.

D.q: A 44-year-old fisherman has a fleshy triangular growth extending from the nasal conjunctiva ONTO the cornea of his right eye. Vision in that eye has dropped slightly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Swelling of the conjunctiva itself, not a discrete fleshy growth.
A fan-shaped lesion that can look similar, but is not the sun-and-wind lesion described.
A yellowish nodule at 3 or 9 o'clock that does NOT touch the cornea.
Correct. The growth crosses the limbus onto the cornea, which is the whole distinction from a pinguecula.

D.q: A 9-year-old girl has a swollen red eyelid, proptosis, pain on eye movement and diplopia. Temperature 39.0°C. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Discharge on oral antibiotics with review in 48 hours
Outpatient oral therapy is for mild pre-septal disease only.
This is a sight- and life-threatening infection.
Admit for intravenous antibiotics and imaging
Correct. All post-septal disease is admitted, and imaging defines the extent. Computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses.
The fever and proptosis indicate infection.

D.q: A 46-year-old man on long-term corticosteroids has glare and trouble reading, and notes his vision improves once his pupils are dilated at the clinic. Which cataract type is this?
opts: Correct — characteristically improves with dilation, more rapid in onset, and classically under fifty.
Age-related, with a myopic shift rather than improvement on dilation.
The commonest PAEDIATRIC type, a white opacity around the nucleus.

Presents later than the first few days.
Presents in the first two weeks but with vesicles and keratitis.

D.q: A 74-year-old woman has sudden painless loss of vision in the left eye. She has had scalp tenderness when brushing her hair and aching in the jaw when chewing for three weeks. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is markedly raised. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Arrange outpatient review in two weeks
Far too slow for a condition that blinds the second eye.
That is the amaurosis fugax pathway.
Arrange temporal artery biopsy and treat once the result is back
Biopsy is confirmatory, but waiting risks the fellow eye.
Correct. Treatment precedes biopsy — the other eye is at risk within days.

D.q: A 15-year-old girl cannot read the board at school but reads comfortably at her desk. Which refractive error is this, and how is the eye shaped?
opts: Blurs at all distances rather than distance alone.
Myopia, with the eye too long
Correct. Light focuses in front of the retina, so distance is blurred and near is clear.
Hyperopia, with the eye too short
Light focuses behind the retina; near vision suffers first.
An age-related near problem, not seen at 15.

D.q: A 65-year-old woman is diagnosed with open-angle glaucoma. Why is she unlikely to have noticed anything?
opts: Central vision fails first and she has adapted
Central acuity is preserved until late.
The pressure is normal in all cases
Pressure is typically raised, though normal-tension disease exists.
The disease causes no field loss at all
It does; the loss is simply unnoticed.
Loss is gradual and the other eye compensates
Correct — which is why it is found on screening rather than by symptoms.

D.q: A 54-year-old woman has painless, oval yellowish plaques on both upper lids near the inner canthus. Vision is normal. What is the most appropriate initial workup?
opts: Imaging has no role in this diagnosis.

It confirms the appearance but misses the systemic point.

opts: Correct. Perforation risk is greatest in the necrotising form rather than uniformly across scleritis.
Presents with pain and vision loss but is not the form named for perforation.
Inflammatory but not the form with the greatest perforation risk.
A superficial and self-limiting condition that does not perforate.

It is bilateral, reflecting raised intracranial pressure.
Papilledema is painful on eye movement
Pain on movement belongs to optic neuritis.
Acuity is preserved in papilledema and reduced in optic neuritis
Correct, and papilledema is bilateral while optic neuritis is usually unilateral with an afferent pupillary defect.

D.q: A 26-year-old woman with idiopathic intracranial hypertension is started on treatment. Which measures are used?
opts: Correct, with serial visual field monitoring.

Associated with cortical cataract and retinopathy.

D.q: A 29-year-old man asks for a bottle of the numbing drops that relieved his corneal abrasion pain in the emergency department. Why should he not be given them?
opts: They cause an allergic reaction in most patients

Repeated use is toxic and delays healing

Not an effect of topical anaesthetic.

Can cause floaters, but the advancing curtain with flashes points to detachment.
Sudden painless loss with widespread haemorrhages, not a progressive curtain preceded by flashes.

Diffuse redness with purulent discharge, not a sector.

Deep boring pain that wakes the patient, with vessels that do NOT blanch.
